The task is to predict the sale prices of 1,459 houses in Ames, Iowa. We learn from 1,460 houses with known prices, and each house has 79 features, such as living area, quality and neighbourhood. Kaggle scores us with the root mean squared error on the log of the price, so a ten percent miss costs the same on a cheap house and on an expensive one.

Our first attempt was a pipeline generated with an AI coding assistant. It scored 0.11745, but we could not explain why each part was there. Since this assignment is about the pathway, we rebuilt everything with two rules: every step changes only one thing, and every step is scored with the same five-fold cross-validation. That way we always knew what each decision was worth.

First, the data. Most houses cost between 100 and 250 thousand dollars, and a few expensive ones make a long tail, so the price has a skewness of 1.88. After a log transform it is 0.12, close to a bell curve. Kaggle also scores on the log price, so we predict the log price and convert back at the end.

Two more findings. A missing value can mean two things. Pool quality is missing for 1,453 houses because they have no pool, so we fill it with None. Lot frontage was simply not recorded, so we fill it with the median. And two very large houses, 524 and 1299, sold for less than 200 thousand dollars. Both were partial sales of unfinished homes, and they come back later in our story.

To compare ideas fairly, we use five-fold cross-validation with the same folds for every step. Each fold of 292 houses is predicted by a model trained on the other 1,168, so every house is predicted once by a model that never saw it. To avoid data leakage, the median filling, scaling and one-hot encoding are refitted inside every fold. Predicting the average price gives an error of 0.408, and a simple Ridge regression gives 0.155.

Then we improved the features one step at a time with the same Ridge model. Predicting the log price and labelling missing values helped a little. Adding total area and house age did nothing, because a linear model can already add columns together. The big jump was step 5: the log of the twenty skewed area features cut the error by twelve percent. Price grows in proportion to size, so on a log scale the relationship becomes a straight line. Thanks. With the features fixed, we compared seven models on the same folds. XGBoost and CatBoost, the two boosting models, were the best at about 0.123, and Random Forest was the worst, even behind Ridge. Random Forest averages trees that are built independently, so after a few hundred trees, more trees stop helping. Boosting adds small trees one after another, and each new tree fixes the error that is still left.

Blending only helps when the models make different mistakes. This heatmap shows how similar their errors are. Ridge, Lasso and ElasticNet make almost the same errors, so we kept only Lasso. We blended Lasso, XGBoost, CatBoost and SVR with equal weights, and the CV error dropped to 0.119, better than any single model. We did not tune the weights, because that would only fit the noise.

Then we submitted to Kaggle. From S1 to S4, our CV and the leaderboard improved together. After that they did not. Our blend, S6, had our best CV score, but on Kaggle it scored 0.12037, worse than our first attempt. Instead of trying more models, we looked at where our errors came from.

We found a blind spot. The two odd houses from our data exploration make up seventeen percent of our squared error. Both fall in fold 3, so our CV never learned from one while predicting the other. The test set has a third house of the same kind, house 2550. Its look-alikes sold for 160 to 185 thousand dollars, but every submission from S1 to S6 predicted between 565 and 891 thousand.

So in step 13 we kept the two houses in training and added one simple feature that flags huge partial sales. Normal cross-validation cannot test this, so we built our own check: hold out one outlier, learn from the other, and predict it. Our predictions went from about four times the true price to under two times. For house 2550, the prediction fell from 643 to 260 thousand dollars, and the other houses barely changed.

We submitted this change only once. It scored 0.11624, our best score and better than our first attempt. For the second question: our biggest improvement on Kaggle was from S1 to S2, a drop of 0.0114, and our cross-validation shows it came mostly from predicting the log price. But the improvement we learned the most from was this last one.

To sum up, we learned three lessons. Change one thing at a time, so you know what each idea is worth. Fit the shape of the data: a log transform gave our biggest gain. And look at the errors: cross-validation has blind spots, and looking at individual houses helped us more than trying more models. [Both] Thank you for watching.
